analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, surgical centers, labs, insurers, and drug middlemen to publish what care actually costs.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Ways and Means Committee on a 25-16 vote in July 2023 but never received a vote by the full House, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required Medicare hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, imaging providers, and clinical labs to post their real prices online — the cash price, the standard list price, and the rates they negotiate with insurers. It would have required employer and individual health plans to give patients a real-time estimate of what they would pay out of pocket for a specific service, to publish their negotiated rates in machine-readable files, and to stop pharmacy benefit managers from hiding drug rebate information from the employers who hire them. It also would have imposed actual penalties — up to $2,000,000 a year for large hospitals that fail to comply — and publicly named violators on the government's Hospital Compare website. The bill cleared the House Ways and Means Committee on a 25-16 vote but never got a vote in the full House or the Senate, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with Medicare, employer coverage, or individual insurance would have been able to see, before getting care, what a hospital charges, what it accepts in cash, and what they personally would owe after deductibles and copays. Employers buying coverage for workers would have received annual machine-readable reports showing exactly how much their pharmacy benefit manager receives in rebates and what drugs actually cost the plan net of rebates. Small hospitals and rural providers would have received lighter treatment: small hospitals face $300-per-day penalties instead of the large-hospital cap, and the Secretary could waive or reduce penalties where enforcement would risk access to care. The bill also appropriated $10,000,000 to HHS to build and monitor the disclosure system.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, employers buying coverage, and researchers

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare-participating hospitals to publish lists of standard charges, discounted cash prices, and (as applicable) payer-specific negotiated rates for every item and service, plus consumer-friendly prices for at least 300 shoppable services, or maintain a public price-estimator tool covering them, starting January 1, 2026.

Backs the requirement with real enforcement: mandatory compliance reviews at least every three years, corrective action plans, per-day civil monetary penalties capped at $2,000,000 for a one-year period for large hospitals (with an added up-to-$1,000,000 increase for repeat willful violators), and public listing of noncompliant hospitals on the Hospital Compare website.
Extends the same cash-price disclosure duty to ambulatory surgical centers (starting 2028), imaging providers (2025), and clinical diagnostic laboratories (2025), each with its own penalty framework.

Rewrites the group health plan transparency rules so that, two years after enactment, plan members can get a real-time estimate of their cost sharing for a specific item or service from a specific provider, including their deductible status and any prior-authorization or step-therapy requirements that apply.

Requires plans and insurers to publish machine-readable in-network rates, out-of-network allowed amounts, and net-of-rebate drug spending, and makes the plan itself attest that the data is complete and accurate.

Bars pharmacy benefit managers from using gag clauses that keep price and rebate information from plan sponsors, and requires an annual machine-readable report covering rebates, fees, formulary placement rationale, and patient out-of-pocket spending by drug and drug class.

Directs the Secretary to make the disclosed information accessible in plain language, with translation and assistive services for people with limited English proficiency and disabilities, and appropriates $10,000,000 for implementation and compliance monitoring.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, imaging providers, clinical labs, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers would have borne the cost of compiling and publishing price data — building public price-estimator tools covering at least 300 shoppable services, quarterly machine-readable rate files, and annual drug-spend reports. Hospitals that repeatedly failed to comply would have faced civil monetary penalties of up to $2,000,000 per year plus an added $1,000,000 for knowing, repeat violations. Insurers would have had to provide real-time personalized cost-sharing estimates. Some compliance cost could be passed on through premiums and charges, and there is a risk that visible negotiated rates make it harder for any single buyer to negotiate below the published norm.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers

drawbacks.text: Disclosure is not a price control: nothing in the bill caps what hospitals, surgical centers, or drug intermediaries may charge, so patients get better information but no guaranteed lower bills.

The compliance costs of compiling, formatting, and updating public price files fall on hospitals and insurers, and providers warn such costs can be passed along to patients through premiums and charges.
The bill allows the Secretary to waive or reduce penalties for providers in rural or underserved areas, creating room for uneven enforcement across the country.

The penalty structure is asymmetric: small hospitals with 30 or fewer beds face a maximum of $300 per day while large hospital systems face up to $2,000,000 per year, which critics of similar frameworks argue is small relative to large systems' revenues.
Sec. 302 extends 'certain direct spending reductions,' a budget offset whose details sit outside the transparency provisions and which the truncated text does not fully specify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real but narrow: patients who take the trouble to look could see prices and out-of-pocket estimates before care, and the codified $2,000,000 annual penalty ceiling with mandatory triennial compliance reviews and public naming of violators would likely have moved hospitals further toward real compliance than the 2022 rule's relatively small penalties did. The costs are administrative (hospitals, surgical centers, labs, imaging providers, and insurers all have to build and maintain public price files and estimator tools), some of which can be passed into premiums and health spending, and some uncertainty about how employers would use newly visible rate data in bargaining. The bill does not directly cap any price or lower any bill, so the benefit depends entirely on consumers and market pressure actually acting on the published data. On balance a modestly pro-patient bill whose promise went unrealized because it never reached the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It got a favorable vote in one House committee but the full House never took it up, and when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 the bill died and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch.

narrative.text: H.R. 4822 was introduced on July 24, 2023 by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO) and referred to four House committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Budget.
Two days after introduction, on July 26, 2023, the Ways and Means Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute (amended) by a recorded vote of 25-16.
On July 28, 2023 the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health within Ways and Means.
On September 29, 2023 the bill was reported (amended) from the Ways and Means Committee as H. Rept. 118-231, Part I.
The bill never received a vote in the full House or Senate, and the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 with the bill still unpassed.
The bill listed zero cosponsors on Congress.gov, so its visible floor-level support never grew beyond its sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers are better off because the bill died: the stronger penalties, mandatory triennial compliance reviews, and PBM gag-clause ban never took effect, leaving the weaker existing transparency rules in place. For ordinary patients, the prospect of enforceable, comparable prices quietly lapsed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers

for.name: Rep. Jason Smith
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 24, 2023 and, as chair, moved it through committee markup within two days.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported (amended) by a recorded vote of 25-16 on July 26, 2023, and formally reported it September 29, 2023 (H. Rept. 118-231).

against.name: House Republican leadership (never scheduled the bill)
against.what_they_did: After the Ways and Means Committee reported the bill in September 2023, no one scheduled it for a vote by the full House in the remaining 15 months of the Congress.

against.name: American Hospital Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed litigation and lobbying against hospital price transparency enforcement generally; the industry has fought the scope of the 2019/2022 transparency rules that this bill would have hardened.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: The brand-drug industry opposes disclosure of rebate and net-price flows, which the bill's PBM reporting provisions would have made routine at the plan level.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote, the Ways and Means committee vote of 25-16, broke along party lines with Republicans in the majority carrying it; the bill never picked up any cosponsors or a floor vote, so its broader support cannot be measured.

industries.note: Hospitals gain a deadline-safe harbor for shoppable services if they run a compliant price-estimator tool, and penalty waivers are available for rural facilities, but the bill puts binding per-day penalties, mandatory triennial audits, and public 'Hospital Compare' shaming behind price disclosure requirements that the existing rule enforces weakly. Hospitals have historically resisted full compliance, so the bill's main cost falls on them.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer group health plans
industries.note: Insurers must build real-time member cost-sharing tools, publish quarterly machine-readable rate files, and personally attest the data is complete and accurate. The bill preserves the existing Transparency in Coverage rule in the interim, so it tightens rather than replaces what they already do; the compliance burden is theirs, while the benefit of comparable plan pricing accrues to consumers and employers.

The bill prohibits PBM gag clauses that block disclosure to plan sponsors and requires annual machine-readable reporting of rebates, fees, formulary placement rationale, and net prices by drug. PBM compensation has long depended on opaque rebate arrangements, so a hard transparency mandate directly threatens that opacity.

industries.industry: Ambulatory surgical centers, imaging providers, and clinical laboratories
industries.note: These providers must publish discounted cash prices for at least 50 shoppable imaging services and listed lab tests, with $300-per-day penalties. Small rural providers can get waivers; large chains cannot. Some of these providers compete on cash prices, so public cash-price data cuts both ways.

Manufacturers are not directly regulated by the bill, but the plan-level reporting of net-of-rebate prices and copay-assistance dollars exposes how rebate flows affect what patients pay. The bill leaves rebate structures themselves intact.
